query: Prior calculations on concentrated alloys examined variations in atomic mass and force constants, temperature-dependent lattice heat transport, or DFT-derived elastic properties coupled to analytical conductivity estimates; some estimates require a Debye temperature. The cited simulations generally represented perfect, defect-free bulk crystals. Experiments below 200 K indicate that lattice and electronic contributions in HfNbTaTiZr can be comparable, while measurements from 300 to 1200 K on a specimen containing 1 wt.% oxygen report total conductivity of 10–17 W/(K m). Available analytical approaches do not capture all relevant atomic-scale complexity in refractory high-entropy alloys, and separate transport studies do not establish a predictive solution for this alloy. Given these constraints, what testable hypothesis could an unspecified new predictive approach make for HfNbTaTiZr without conflating lattice and electronic heat transport? Explain why it should outperform earlier approaches, quantify the expected improvement, define its temperature and sample applicability limits, identify supporting observations from the cited work, and specify decisive comparisons with low- and high-temperature measurements that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: A new predictive approach that separately accounts for atomic-scale lattice distortions and force‐constant fluctuations—using a combined DFT/MD/machine‐learning framework—will decouple lattice from electronic heat transport in HfNbTaTiZr. Specifically, it will predict that (i) the lattice (phonon) thermal conductivity remains nearly constant (approximately 4–7 W/(K·m)) at low temperatures (e.g., below 200 K) despite rising temperature, while (ii) the electronic thermal conductivity exhibits a mild temperature dependence and becomes dominant above ~300 K. In turn, the total thermal conductivity, when recombined, will be predicted with an approximate 30% improvement in accuracy over previous Debye-based approaches—yielding values in the range 10–17 W/(K·m) at high temperatures (300–1200 K) for oxygen-free samples.
generation.material_initial_state: Defect-free, single-phase bulk HfNbTaTiZr alloy with minimal extrinsic impurities (especially oxygen) to ensure results reflect intrinsic behavior.
generation.intervention: Application of the new predictive protocol that independently models the phonon dynamics (capturing lattice distortions and force-constant fluctuations) and electronic transport properties using integrated DFT, molecular dynamics, and machine learning techniques.
generation.conditions: Measurements and predictions are to be evaluated from cryogenic temperatures (~50 K) up to high temperatures (1200 K); comparisons should be made on samples prepared under oxygen-free conditions as well as oxygen-doped variants to explore potential shifts in electronic contribution.
generation.structural_mediator: Local lattice distortions and fluctuations in interatomic force constants arising from the chemical complexity of the alloy.
generation.mechanism: By isolating the effects of static lattice distortions from electronic scattering, the model accurately captures the distinct temperature dependencies of phonon and electron transport channels. This decoupling allows improved predictions over conventional methods that conflate these effects, thereby reducing error in total thermal conductivity estimates.
generation.predicted_outcome: The model will predict a nearly invariant lattice thermal conductivity (≈4–7 W/(K·m)) at temperatures below 200 K, with a clear transition at higher temperatures where electronic thermal conductivity rises to dominate the total heat transport, resulting in overall conductivity between 10 and 17 W/(K·m) at temperatures of 300–1200 K, in agreement with key experimental observations.
generation.baseline: Earlier approaches generally used Debye-temperature based and mean-field models that conflated lattice and electronic contributions, often overestimating lattice thermal conductivity and lacking accurate temperature dependence.
generation.boundary: The predictions should hold for well-prepared, defect-free single-phase bulk HfNbTaTiZr alloys. Significant deviations are expected for samples with high levels of defects, grain boundary scattering, or non-ideal microstructures.
generation.uncertainty: The estimated 30% improvement in predictive accuracy is approximate and may vary with subtle changes in sample purity and processing. Detailed quantification of temperature-dependent crossovers between lattice and electronic contributions remains to be refined through experimental validation.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize high-quality, single-phase HfNbTaTiZr samples and perform temperature-dependent thermal conductivity measurements. Use independent techniques to separate lattice and electronic contributions (e.g., applying the Wiedemann–Franz law to concurrent electrical resistivity measurements for the electronic part and transient thermal techniques for the lattice part) over a temperature range from 50 K to 1200 K. Compare these measured values against the predictions offered by the new decoupled model.
measurements: Total thermal conductivity as a function of temperature
Lattice (phonon) thermal conductivity isolated at low temperatures (below 200 K)
Electronic thermal conductivity using resistivity and Lorenz number estimation
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis will be falsified if: (a) the measured lattice thermal conductivity at T < 200 K does not remain nearly constant around 4–7 W/(K·m); (b) the model fails to capture the predicted rise of electronic conductivity and its dominance above ~300 K; or (c) the total thermal conductivity falls significantly outside the 10–17 W/(K·m) range in the high-temperature regime, indicating that the decoupling of contributions has not been correctly achieved.

cited_evidence.text: The primary objective of this study is to investigate the impact of bond length and atomic size disorder on structural and mechanical properties. The resulting lattice distortion plays a pivotal role in various aspects of compositionally complex and high-entropy alloys, as evidenced by prior research (). To isolate the effects of atomic size variations and the resulting lattice distortions on thermodynamic behavior, we intentionally neglect the influence of bond strength or stiffness variations among alloy components. Our approach is rooted in a statistical mechanics treatment of both distortions arising from thermal fluctuations in bond length and those associated with bond length disorder. We explore these phenomena within a simple 2D model and subsequently validate the emergent features within a 3D crystal lattice using MD simulations.

We have also calculated the standard deviation of the nearest-neighbor distances for several experimentally realized HEAs. Specifically, for the FCC Cantor alloy (CoCrMnFeNi), we find Σ=0.0303, and for FCC CoCrCuFeNi, Σ=0.0294 (refer to Table S2 for more details). As previously discussed, bond length disorder effectively elevates the temperature above its actual value. At room temperature, this amounts to an increase of 42% for CoCrMnFeNi and 41% for CoCrCuFeNi (details are available in Table S2). At 1,000 K, the influence of bond length disorder is more modest, effectively raising the temperature by 12% for both alloys. It is crucial to highlight that while bond length disorder significantly impacts thermodynamic properties at lower temperatures, its effect on elastic constants and melting temperatures is much less pronounced. Moreover, these impacts are generally subdued in FCC HEAs owing to their lower levels of local lattice disorder (Σ≤5%) (, ) (see Figs S18 and S23). cited_evidence.kind: web:Conductive and wear performance of the NbMoTaW coatings on AFM probe tips
cited_evidence.text: In summary, this study has established a conductivity model for the HEA system Nb-Mo-Ta-W, designed alloy compositions with high conductivity and wear resistance, which can be applied to enhance the atomic-level resolution and lifespan of atomic force microscope probes. By adjusting the composition, a refractory high-entropy material of Nb15Mo35Ta15W35 was endowed with both high hardness and electrical conductivity. We indicate that the conductivity of Nb-Mo-Ta-W HEAs can be modulated through the cocktail effect but tends to differ by an order of magnitude compared to linear combinations. The reasons for the decrease in conductivity are attributed to changes in the plasma frequency and relaxation time resulting from lattice distortions, alterations in the effective mass and density of free electrons, and variations in the crystalline size after the formation of HEAs.

Figure 3 shows the temperature dependence of the measured κ, and the derived values of κe and κg for NiCoFeCrMn and NiCoFeCrPd. One distinct feature of the concentrated alloys, relative to pure metals, is that in a pure metal the total thermal conductivity is dominated by κe, and κg is usually negligible. However, in concentrated alloys, κg seems to dominate at low temperatures and is comparable with κe at about room temperature. Chemical disorder appears to scatter electrons more effectively than phonons. In addition, in pure metals κ starts decreasing at a few tens of K, while in concentrated alloys κ keeps increasing up to at least 300 K (see Table 3). One major reason is that, due to the large and nearly constant resistivity of these complex alloys, κe almost linearly increases with temperature up to 300 K, which is very different from the behavior in pure metals. The theoretical description of the temperature dependence of κg for disordered alloys has been challenging. cited_evidence.text: Thermal conductivity is composed of two parts, the electronic thermal conductivity (ke) and the lattice thermal conductivity (kL). The electronic thermal conductivity was calculated using the Wiedemann–Franz law [,], where L was approximated by the Lorenz number L0 that takes the value 2.44 × 108 WΩK−1. Whereas the deviation of the L/L0 ratio from one is still an open question for nanoscale materials [], it seems that the deviation from the Wiedemann–Franz law occurs mainly at low temperature (well below 300 K) where lattice vibrations increase the L/L0 ratio above 1. However, this tendency can also be counteracted by electronic corrections, leading finally to a small change of the L/L0 ratio (between 0.8 and 1.2, at most). For bulk compounds, the same effects can occur. Therefore, we are confident that the conclusions presented hereafter should not change drastically with L.
